Frontal.name: Frontal Bone
Frontal.description: A thick, shell-like bone forming the anterior roof of the cranium and the forehead. It contains the frontal sinuses and forms the superior margin of the orbits (eye sockets). It articulates with the parietal bones at the coronal suture and with the sphenoid, ethmoid, and nasal bones. Functionally, it protects the brain's frontal lobes and supports facial structure.

Parietal.name: Parietal Bone
Parietal.description: Large, quadrilateral, paired bones forming the bulk of the cranial vault's roof and sides. They articulate with each other at the sagittal suture, the frontal bone at the coronal suture, and the occipital bone at the lambdoid suture. Their internal surface features grooves for the middle meningeal artery, making them clinically significant in head trauma cases.

Temporal.name: Temporal Bone
Temporal.description: Complex bones at the lateral base of the skull. They house the internal auditory meatus, middle ear ossicles, and the cochlea. Landmarks include the mastoid process (muscle attachment), the zygomatic process (forming the cheek arch), and the mandibular fossa, which forms the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) with the lower jaw.

Occipital.name: Occipital Bone
Occipital.description: Forms the posterior and inferior base of the neurocranium. It contains the foramen magnum, the primary opening for the spinal cord to connect to the brainstem. It features the occipital condyles, which articulate with the Atlas (C1) to allow for nodding motions, and the external occipital protuberance for neck muscle attachment.

Ethmoid.name: Ethmoid Bone
Ethmoid.description: A light, spongy, cubical bone located between the orbits at the roof of the nose. It features the cribriform plate, perforated with tiny holes for olfactory nerves to pass to the brain. Its crista galli serves as an attachment for the falx cerebri (brain membrane), and its perpendicular plate forms the superior part of the nasal septum.

Sphenoid.name: Sphenoid Bone
Sphenoid.description: Known as the "keystone" of the cranial floor because it articulates with all other cranial bones. Butterfly-shaped, it contains the sella turcica (a saddle-like depression housing the pituitary gland). It features the optic canals for the optic nerves and the greater/lesser wings that form part of the orbits and middle cranial fossa.

Nasal.name: Nasal Bone
Nasal.description: Two small, oblong bones placed side-by-side that form the bridge of the nose. While small, they provide the primary rigid support for the superior portion of the nose; the remainder of the nasal structure is composed of flexible hyaline cartilage.

Lacrimal.name: Lacrimal Bone
Lacrimal.description: The smallest and most fragile facial bones, located in the medial wall of each orbit. They feature the lacrimal sulcus, which houses the lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct, allowing tears to drain from the eye surface into the nasal cavity.

Zygomatic.name: Zygomatic Bone
Zygomatic.description: The "cheekbones" forming the lateral wall and floor of the orbits. They articulate with the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and maxillary bones. They provide the structural "corners" of the face and serve as the origin for the masseter muscle, essential for powerful jaw closure.

Maxilla.name: Maxilla
Maxilla.description: The upper jawbones that form the central facial skeleton. They house the upper teeth within the alveolar process, form the floor of the orbits, and the lateral walls of the nasal cavity. Each maxilla contains a large maxillary sinus. They articulate with every facial bone except the mandible, providing the rigid foundation for the mid-face.

Mandible.name: Mandible
Mandible.description: The largest, strongest, and only movable bone of the skull. It consists of a horizontal body housing the lower teeth and two vertical rami. The condylar process articulates with the temporal bone (TMJ), while the coronoid process serves as a lever for the temporalis muscle during chewing. It is the primary structural component of the lower face.

Vomer.name: Vomer
Vomer.description: A thin, flat, plow-shaped bone situated in the midsagittal line. It articulates with the ethmoid bone and the maxillae/palatines to form the inferior and posterior portion of the bony nasal septum, which provides the primary structural division of the nasal airway.

Palatine.name: Palatine Bone
Palatine.description: L-shaped bones located at the posterior of the nasal cavity. They form the posterior third of the hard palate (roof of the mouth), part of the nasal floor, and a tiny portion of the orbital floor. Failure of these bones to fuse correctly during development can contribute to a cleft palate.

Inferior Nasal Concha.name: Inferior Nasal Concha
Inferior Nasal Concha.description: Thin, curved, scroll-like bones projecting from the lateral walls of the nasal cavity. Unlike the superior/middle conchae (part of the ethmoid), these are independent bones. They function to create turbulence in inhaled air, increasing surface area for warming, moistening, and filtering.

Malleus.name: Malleus
Malleus.description: The \"hammer\"; the largest of the middle ear ossicles. The \"handle\" is attached to the internal surface of the tympanic membrane (eardrum), while the head articulates with the incus. It converts sound waves into mechanical vibrations.

Incus.name: Incus
Incus.description: The \"anvil\"; the middle bone of the ossicular chain. It acts as a lever, receiving vibrations from the malleus and transmitting them to the stapes. This chain of bones amplifies sound pressure before it reaches the fluid-filled inner ear.

Stapes.name: Stapes
Stapes.description: The "stirrup"; the smallest bone in the human body. Its footplate occupies the oval window of the cochlea. It acts like a piston, pushing against the inner ear fluid to trigger the neural signals interpreted as sound.

Hyoid.name: Hyoid Bone
Hyoid.description: A U-shaped bone in the anterior neck between the mandible and larynx. It is the only bone in the body that does not articulate with any other bone; it is suspended by muscles and ligaments. It serves as a movable base for the tongue and an attachment point for muscles that elevate the larynx during swallowing.

Vertebra_C1.name: Atlas (C1)
Vertebra_C1.description: Supports the skull. Lacks a body; consists of anterior and posterior arches with lateral masses.

Vertebra_C2.name: Axis (C2)
Vertebra_C2.description: Has an odontoid process (dens) that acts as a pivot for head rotation relative to the atlas.

Vertebra_C3.name: Cervical Vertebra (C3)
Vertebra_C3.description: Third cervical vertebra with typical cervical features.

Vertebra_C7.name: Cervical Vertebra (C7)
Vertebra_C7.description: Seventh cervical vertebra. Has a prominent spinous process palpable at the base of the neck.

Vertebra_T1.name: Thoracic Vertebra (T1)
Vertebra_T1.description: First thoracic vertebra. Articulates with the first pair of ribs.

Vertebra_T12.name: Thoracic Vertebra (T12)
Vertebra_T12.description: Twelfth thoracic vertebra, the lowest thoracic vertebra.

Vertebra_L1.name: Lumbar Vertebra (L1)
Vertebra_L1.description: First lumbar vertebra. Largest of the lumbar vertebrae.

Vertebra_L5.name: Lumbar Vertebra (L5)
Vertebra_L5.description: Fifth lumbar vertebra. Articulates with the sacrum below.

Sacrum.name: Sacrum
Sacrum.description: Large triangular bone formed by fusion of 5 sacral vertebrae. Base of the spine, articulates with pelvis.

Coccyx.name: Coccyx
Coccyx.description: Small triangular bone formed by fusion of 3-5 coccygeal vertebrae at the base of spine.

Rib_1_Right.name: First Rib (Right)
Rib_1_Right.description: Shortest and most curved rib, articulates with T1 vertebra and sternum.

Rib_2_Right.name: Second Rib (Right)
Rib_2_Right.description: Second rib, articulates with T2 vertebra and sternum.

Rib_3_Right.name: Third Rib (Right)
Rib_3_Right.description: Third rib, articulates with T3 vertebra.

Rib_7_Right.name: Seventh Rib (Right)
Rib_7_Right.description: Seventh rib, the last true rib.

Rib_12_Right.name: Twelfth Rib (Right)
Rib_12_Right.description: Twelfth rib, the last and shortest floating rib.

Rib_1_Left.name: First Rib (Left)
Rib_1_Left.description: Shortest and most curved rib on left side.

Rib_7_Left.name: Seventh Rib (Left)
Rib_7_Left.description: Seventh rib on left side, the last true rib.

Rib_8_Left.name: Eighth Rib (Left)
Rib_8_Left.description: Eighth rib on left side, a false rib.

Rib_9_Left.name: Ninth Rib (Left)
Rib_9_Left.description: Ninth rib on left side, a false rib.

Rib_10_Left.name: Tenth Rib (Left)
Rib_10_Left.description: Tenth rib on left side, a false rib.

Rib_11_Left.name: Eleventh Rib (Left)
Rib_11_Left.description: Eleventh rib on left side, floating rib.

Rib_12_Left.name: Twelfth Rib (Left)
Rib_12_Left.description: Twelfth rib on left side, the last and shortest floating rib.

Sternum.name: Sternum
Sternum.description: Flat bone in center of chest connecting ribs and clavicles. Protects heart and lungs.

Ilium.name: Ilium
Ilium.description: Largest part of the os coxa (hip bone) formed by the fusion of the Ilium, Ischium, and Pubis. Forms the lateral and superior part of the pelvis. The three bones meet at the acetabulum, the deep socket for the femur.

Ischium.name: Ischium
Ischium.description: Lower and posterior part of the os coxa. Forms the ischial tuberosities (sitting bones), which are the points of contact when sitting.

Pubis.name: Pubis
Pubis.description: Anterior and inferior part of the os coxa. Two pubes meet at the pubic symphysis anteriorly and are fused with the sacrum posteriorly to form the bony pelvis.

ScapulaRight.name: Scapula (Right)
ScapulaRight.description: The \"shoulder blade\"; a flat, triangular bone on the posterolateral aspect of the thorax (ribs 2-7). Key landmarks include the glenoid cavity (socket for the humerus), the acromion (the high point of the shoulder), and the coronoid process. It provides an expansive surface for the attachment of the rotator cuff muscles, facilitating complex shoulder mobility.

ScapulaLeft.name: Scapula (Left)
ScapulaLeft.description: The \"shoulder blade\"; a flat, triangular bone on the posterolateral aspect of the thorax (ribs 2-7). Key landmarks include the glenoid cavity (socket for the humerus), the acromion (the high point of the shoulder), and the coronoid process. It provides an expansive surface for the attachment of the rotator cuff muscles, facilitating complex shoulder mobility.

Clavicle Right.name: Clavicle (Right)
Clavicle Right.description: The \"collarbone\"; a doubly-curved long bone that serves as a horizontal strut connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton. It articulates medially with the sternum (sternoclavicular joint) and laterally with the acromion of the scapula (acromioclavicular joint). It acts as a shock absorber and provides the only bony attachment between the trunk and the arm.

Clavicle Left.name: Clavicle (Left)
Clavicle Left.description: The \"collarbone\"; a doubly-curved long bone that serves as a horizontal strut connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton. It articulates medially with the sternum (sternoclavicular joint) and laterally with the acromion of the scapula (acromioclavicular joint). It acts as a shock absorber and provides the only bony attachment between the trunk and the arm.

Humerus Right.name: Humerus (Right)
Humerus Right.description: The longest and largest bone of the upper limb. Proximally, its smooth head fits into the glenoid cavity. Distally, it features the trochlea and capitulum for articulation with the ulna and radius at the elbow. Significant landmarks include the deltoid tuberosity for muscle attachment and the bicipital groove which houses the long head of the biceps tendon.

Humerus Left.name: Humerus (Left)
Humerus Left.description: The longest and largest bone of the upper limb. Proximally, its smooth head fits into the glenoid cavity. Distally, it features the trochlea and capitulum for articulation with the ulna and radius at the elbow. Significant landmarks include the deltoid tuberosity for muscle attachment and the bicipital groove which houses the long head of the biceps tendon.

Radius Right.name: Radius (Right)
Radius Right.description: The lateral bone of the forearm, situated on the thumb side. Its disc-shaped head articulates with the humerus and the radial notch of the ulna. It is the primary bone involved in the wrist joint (radiocarpal joint). Its unique ability to pivot over the ulna allows for pronation (palm down) and supination (palm up).

Radius Left.name: Radius (Left)
Radius Left.description: The lateral bone of the forearm, situated on the thumb side. Its disc-shaped head articulates with the humerus and the radial notch of the ulna. It is the primary bone involved in the wrist joint (radiocarpal joint). Its unique ability to pivot over the ulna allows for pronation (palm down) and supination (palm up).

Ulna Right.name: Ulna (Right)
Ulna Right.description: The medial bone of the forearm (pinky side). It is longer than the radius and acts as the stabilizing bone. Its hook-like olecranon process forms the bony point of the elbow and fits into the olecranon fossa of the humerus. It articulates with the radius proximally and distally but does not articulate directly with the carpal bones of the wrist.

Ulna Left.name: Ulna (Left)
Ulna Left.description: The medial bone of the forearm (pinky side). It is longer than the radius and acts as the stabilizing bone. Its hook-like olecranon process forms the bony point of the elbow and fits into the olecranon fossa of the humerus. It articulates with the radius proximally and distally but does not articulate directly with the carpal bones of the wrist.

Femur Right.name: Femur (Right)
Femur Right.description: The thigh bone; the longest, heaviest, and strongest bone in the body. Its spherical head fits into the acetabulum, while its neck—a common site for fractures—projects the shaft laterally. Distally, the medial and lateral condyles articulate with the tibia and patella. It is the primary load-bearing bone of the lower body.

Femur Left.name: Femur (Left)
Femur Left.description: The thigh bone; the longest, heaviest, and strongest bone in the body. Its spherical head fits into the acetabulum, while its neck—a common site for fractures—projects the shaft laterally. Distally, the medial and lateral condyles articulate with the tibia and patella. It is the primary load-bearing bone of the lower body.

Patella Right.name: Patella (Right)
Patella Right.description: The \"kneecap\"; a large, flat sesamoid bone triangular in shape. It is situated within the quadriceps femoris tendon and articulates with the patellar surface of the femur. Its primary function is to increase the mechanical advantage (leverage) of the quadriceps muscle during leg extension and to protect the knee joint.

Patella Left.name: Patella (Left)
Patella Left.description: The \"kneecap\"; a large, flat sesamoid bone triangular in shape. It is situated within the quadriceps femoris tendon and articulates with the patellar surface of the femur. Its primary function is to increase the mechanical advantage (leverage) of the quadriceps muscle during leg extension and to protect the knee joint.

Tibia Right.name: Tibia (Right)
Tibia Right.description: The \"shinbone\"; the second-longest bone in the body and the primary weight-bearing bone of the lower leg. It articulates proximally with the femoral condyles to form the knee and distally with the talus to form the ankle. Its medial malleolus forms the inner prominence of the ankle.

Tibia Left.name: Tibia (Left)
Tibia Left.description: The \"shinbone\"; the second-longest bone in the body and the primary weight-bearing bone of the lower leg. It articulates proximally with the femoral condyles to form the knee and distally with the talus to form the ankle. Its medial malleolus forms the inner prominence of the ankle.

Fibula Right.name: Fibula (Right)
Fibula Right.description: A slender, non-weight-bearing bone on the lateral side of the tibia. Its proximal head does not reach the knee joint, but its distal end, the lateral malleolus, forms the outer prominence of the ankle and provides critical lateral stability to the talocrural (ankle) joint. It serves as a major origin point for leg muscles.

Fibula Left.name: Fibula (Left)
Fibula Left.description: A slender, non-weight-bearing bone on the lateral side of the tibia. Its proximal head does not reach the knee joint, but its distal end, the lateral malleolus, forms the outer prominence of the ankle and provides critical lateral stability to the talocrural (ankle) joint. It serves as a major origin point for leg muscles.
